# 13. County need layers

Almost every opportunity here is statewide, so joining county data straight to opportunities
would give a near-constant column. Instead, county data describe **program domains**: each
domain's need index is a county's average percentile rank across that domain's indicators, and
an opportunity inherits its domain's map. The tool shows these with a boundary overlay for
counties, congressional districts, census tracts, and places.

```{r need-maps}
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-width: 9
#| code-summary: "Need index by domain"
ci <- build_county_indicators()
need <- build_domain_need(ci)
counties <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_CACHE_GEO, "nc_county_2023.rds"))
need_long <- imap_dfr(need, function(d, id) if (!isTRUE(d$available)) NULL else
  tibble(fips = names(d$index), index = unlist(d$index), domain = DOMAINS[[id]]))
counties |> select(GEOID) |> inner_join(need_long, by = c("GEOID" = "fips")) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = index), color = "white", linewidth = .1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cde2fb", high = "#0d366b", labels = percent, name = "Need\npercentile") +
  facet_wrap(~ str_wrap(domain, 40), ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Relative need by program domain, NC counties",
       caption = str_wrap(paste0("Indicators: CDC PLACES, ACS 2023 5-year, HRSA HPSA designations, OpenFEMA declarations, NCHS model-based drug poisoning death rates (",
                        min(OVERDOSE_YEARS), "-", max(OVERDOSE_YEARS), "). Color is each county's average percentile rank across its domain's indicators."), 110)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9, margin = margin(b = 4)),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, margin = margin(b = 10)),
        plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, color = pal$gray, size = 8.5, margin = margin(t = 10)),
        panel.spacing = unit(10, "pt"), plot.margin = margin(8, 8, 8, 8))
```

::: {.takeaway}
Need is not one map. Poverty-driven domains (food, children, maternal health) concentrate in the
east and southeast; overdose concentrates in the mountains; preparedness follows the hurricane coast.
:::

**Every indicator behind those maps.** Each source is shown on its own, as a percentile rank
across the 100 counties (darker = higher need), so a reader can see which dataset drives each domain.

```{r indicator-maps}
#| fig-height: 9.2
#| fig-width: 10
#| code-summary: "Each county indicator mapped"
ind <- imap_dfr(domain_indicators(), ~ tibble(var = names(.x), label = unname(.x))) |> distinct(var, .keep_all = TRUE)
ind <- bind_rows(ind, tibble(var = "veteran_share", label = "Veterans as a share of adults (ACS)"))
counties |> select(GEOID) |>
  inner_join(ci |> select(fips, any_of(ind$var)) |>
               pivot_longer(-fips, names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
               group_by(var) |> mutate(pct = percent_rank(value)) |> ungroup(),
             by = c("GEOID" = "fips")) |>
  left_join(ind, by = "var") |>
  mutate(label = str_wrap(label, 34)) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = pct), color = "white", linewidth = .05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e3eefb", high = "#0d366b", labels = percent, name = "County\npercentile", na.value = "#eeeeee") +
  facet_wrap(~ label, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "The raw indicators, one map each",
       caption = "Sources in parentheses. FEMA counts declarations since 2016; HRSA counts designated shortage areas; PLACES values are model-based adult prevalence.") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 3, t = 6)),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, margin = margin(b = 10)),
        plot.title.position = "plot", plot.caption.position = "plot",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, color = pal$gray, size = 8.5, margin = margin(t = 10)),
        legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(8, 8, 8, 8))
```

```{r need-indicators}
#| code-summary: "Indicators behind each domain"
imap_dfr(domain_indicators(), ~ tibble(domain = DOMAINS[[.y]], indicator = unname(.x))) |> dt(pageLength = 20)
```

```{r overdose-map}
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
#| code-summary: "Drug poisoning death rates by county"
counties |> select(GEOID) |> left_join(select(ci, fips, overdose_rate), by = c("GEOID" = "fips")) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = overdose_rate), color = "white", linewidth = .15) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cde2fb", high = "#0d366b", name = "Deaths per\n100,000") +
  labs(title = "Overdose deaths concentrate in the mountains and along the coast",
       subtitle = paste0("Drug poisoning death rate, ", min(OVERDOSE_YEARS), "-", max(OVERDOSE_YEARS), " average (NCHS model-based county estimates)")) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13, margin = margin(b = 4)), plot.subtitle = element_text(color = pal$gray, margin = margin(b = 8)),
        plot.title.position = "plot", plot.margin = margin(8, 8, 8, 8))
```

::: {.takeaway}
The western mountain counties and parts of the southeast coast have the highest overdose death
rates, a different set of counties from where poverty-driven need is highest.
:::

```{r need-correlation}
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-width: 7
#| code-summary: "Do the need layers point to the same counties?"
nm <- need_long |> mutate(domain = str_wrap(domain, 24)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = domain, values_from = index)
cm <- cor(select(nm, -fips), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
as.data.frame(as.table(cm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", Freq)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal$red, mid = "#f5f5f3", high = pal$blue, midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Correlation") +
  labs(title = "Most need layers point to the same counties; overdose does not",
       subtitle = str_wrap("Correlation of county need indices between domains. Overdose need runs opposite to the poverty-driven layers, and behavioral health is largely independent, so one 'high-need county' list would mislead.", 80),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

::: {.takeaway}
This is why the tool maps need per domain instead of ranking "high-need counties" once: a
substance-use grant and a nutrition grant point a writer to different parts of the state.
:::

# 14. The tool

The same file judges would open by double-click, embedded here. It recomputes every tier in the
browser as settings change.

**Using the tool.** A writer can describe their situation in plain English, for example "one month,
match with approval, awards of at least $1 million, reach the most people". The tool then sets:
- runway, match authority and staff;
- minimum award;
- program priorities;
- what matters most for the impact score.

Each setting it changes appears as a chip that can be undone. Example buttons apply ready-made
scenarios in one click, presets set whole personas, and a "Larger text" button enlarges everything
for a projector.

**Who an opportunity reaches.** Each opportunity's detail panel has a "Who this reaches in NC"
section, and the map has a matching layer. They show:
- where the population it serves lives: the counties with the most people and with the highest share of residents;
- the split between rural, suburban and urban counties (NC Rural Center density definition);
- counts by congressional district (ACS 2019-2023, 118th Congress districts).

This describes where people live, not where a statewide award would be spent. It is most informative
for the opportunities labeled with a specific group (children, veterans, adults in mental distress,
recent births and others). The labeler marked most opportunities as serving all residents or as
system-level work with no direct beneficiaries.

```{r embed-tool}
#| code-summary: "Embed outs/grant-triage-tool.html"
if (file.exists(TOOL_HTML_OUT)) {
  tags$iframe(srcdoc = paste(readLines(TOOL_HTML_OUT, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), collapse = "\n"),
              style = "width:100%; height:1100px; border:1px solid #E4E7EC; border-radius:8px;",
              title = "NC Grant Triage tool")
} else {
  HTML('<div class="pending">Build the tool first: <code>Rscript src/tool/build_tool.R</code></div>')
}
```

## Top results

The competition asks for a top results list with a one-line rationale per opportunity tied to the
match criteria. This is it: every opportunity in Tiers 1-3 of the tool's opening scenario (the
interview persona: about a month of runway, supervisor approves match, one FTE, forecasts
included), for DHHS and DMVA, ordered by tier and then by impact score with equal weights. Each
line walks the five criteria in order: can we apply, do we have the capabilities, is there runway,
what is the award, is the match survivable. Tier 4 (partner-led research) is excluded here; it is
in the tool. Also saved as `outs/top_results.xlsx`.

```{r top-results}
#| code-summary: "Top results list (computed by tiering.js)"
top_results <- bind_rows(build_top_results(payload, "DHHS"), build_top_results(payload, "DMVA"))
top_results |>
  transmute(agency, tier, impact = impact_score, opportunity = title, deadline, rationale) |>
  dt(pageLength = 25)
```

`r nrow(filter(top_results, agency == "DHHS"))` opportunities make the DHHS list:
`r sum(top_results$agency == "DHHS" & top_results$tier == 1)` the writer can start,
`r sum(top_results$agency == "DHHS" & top_results$tier == 2)` that need a supervisor or division, and
`r sum(top_results$agency == "DHHS" & top_results$tier == 3)` that need the secretary or legislature.
`r sum(top_results$agency == "DHHS" & top_results$status == "forecasted")` of them are forecasts: the
posted pipeline for a DHHS writer on `r format(REF_DATE_DEFAULT, "%B %d")` is thin, and most of the
actionable work is preparing for what is about to post.

## Reach and intensity

"People reached" in the impact score comes from the population the labeler says an opportunity
serves, counted for North Carolina from the ACS and CDC PLACES:

```{r populations}
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-summary: "Size of each target population in NC"
map_dfr(payload$populations, ~ tibble(label = .x$label, n = .x$n %||% NA_real_, source = .x$source %||% "")) |>
  filter(!is.na(n), n > 0) |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, label)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal$blue, width = .7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale(), accuracy = .1)(n)), hjust = -.15, size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .16))) +
  labs(title = "Who an opportunity can reach: from 127,000 to 10.6 million",
       subtitle = "North Carolina population for each target group the labeler can choose",
       x = "People in NC", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r reach-static}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "People served vs dollars per person, opening scenario"
rv <- opening |> filter(placement == "pile") |>
  mutate(o = map(opportunity_number, function(n) keep(opps, ~ .x$number == n)[[1]]),
         people = map_dbl(o, ~ .x$people_est %||% NA_real_),
         award = map_dbl(o, ~ .x$award_estimate_usd %||% NA_real_),
         pop = map_chr(o, ~ .x$target_population %||% NA_character_)) |>
  filter(!is.na(people), !is.na(award), people > 0) |>
  mutate(per_person = award / people, tier = factor(paste("Tier", tier)))
ggplot(rv, aes(people, per_person, color = tier, shape = tier)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = .7, position = position_jitter(width = .06, height = 0, seed = SEED)) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()), expand = expansion(mult = .08)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_dollar(accuracy = .001, drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Tier 1" = pal$tier1, "Tier 2" = pal$tier2, "Tier 3" = pal$tier3, "Tier 4" = pal$gray), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Tier 1" = 16, "Tier 2" = 15, "Tier 3" = 17, "Tier 4" = 18), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Reach and intensity are different axes, never one score",
       subtitle = str_wrap(paste0(nrow(rv), " opportunities in the opening scenario with an estimated population. Horizontal: people in the population served (upper bound). Vertical: award divided by that population."), 95),
       x = "People in the population served, NC (log)", y = "Dollars per person (log)",
       caption = "Points are spread slightly sideways so overlapping values stay visible.") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")
```

Opportunities serving the same population share a horizontal position, so they stack in columns; the
estimate is only as good as the population the labeler chose, which the team could not score
automatically (section 12).

**Where each population lives.** The same counts, split by the NC Rural Center's density grouping
(rural = 250 people per square mile or fewer; urban = more than 750) and by congressional district:

```{r population-geography}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-summary: "Rural, suburban and urban share of each target population"
rur <- unlist(payload$community$county_rurality)
rur_lab <- c(rural = "Rural", suburban = "Suburban / regional city", urban = "Urban")
imap_dfr(payload$populations, function(p, id) if (is.null(p$county) || !length(p$county)) NULL else
  tibble(label = p$label, fips = names(p$county), n = unlist(p$county))) |>
  mutate(rurality = factor(rur_lab[rur[fips]], levels = rev(rur_lab))) |>
  count(label, rurality, wt = n) |>
  group_by(label) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n), rural_share = sum(share[rurality == "Rural"])) |> ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(share, fct_reorder(label, rural_share), fill = rurality)) +
  geom_col(width = .7, color = "white", linewidth = .3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Rural" = "#1baf7a", "Suburban / regional city" = "#6da7ec", "Urban" = "#184f95"),
                    breaks = unname(rur_lab), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .02))) +
  labs(title = "Hazard-exposed and shortage-area residents are the most rural",
       subtitle = paste0("Share of each target population living in NC's ", sum(rur == "rural"), " rural, ",
                         sum(rur == "suburban"), " suburban and ", sum(rur == "urban"), " urban counties"),
       x = "Share of the population", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r population-districts}
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-summary: "Target populations by congressional district"
dn <- unlist(payload$community$district_names)
imap_dfr(payload$populations, function(p, id) if (is.null(p$district) || id == "all_residents") NULL else
  tibble(label = p$label, geoid = names(p$district), n = unlist(p$district))) |>
  filter(label %in% c("Children under 18", "Adults 65 and older", "Veterans", "People below the poverty line")) |>
  mutate(label = recode(label, "People below the poverty line" = "Below poverty", "Adults 65 and older" = "Adults 65+")) |>
  mutate(district = factor(str_remove(dn[geoid], "Congressional "), levels = str_remove(dn[order(as.integer(names(dn)))], "Congressional "))) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_rev(district))) +
  geom_col(fill = pal$blue, width = .7) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()), breaks = scales::breaks_extended(3), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "Districts hold roughly equal people, but not equal needs",
       subtitle = str_wrap(paste0("ACS 2019-2023 counts by congressional district. ", payload$community$district_note), 78),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8), panel.spacing.x = unit(18, "pt"))
```

::: {.takeaway}
Each district has about 750,000 residents, yet veterans are concentrated in districts 3 and 9
and older adults in district 11. A grant for one population
reaches very different parts of the state than a grant for another.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Large statewide programs spread cents per person across millions; a few small programs put
$10-100 per person into a narrow group. The tool lets the writer choose which matters more instead
of blending the two.
:::

# 15. Evaluation

## What landed in the piles

```{r spot-check}
#| code-summary: "Opening-scenario results for hand spot-checking"
opening |> filter(placement == "pile", tier <= 3) |>
  left_join(labels %||% tibble(opportunity_number = character(), labeled = logical(), has_nofo = logical()), by = "opportunity_number") |>
  transmute(tier, opportunity = opportunity_title,
            `labeled by model` = coalesce(labeled, FALSE),
            `full announcement read` = coalesce(has_nofo, FALSE), reason = tier_reason) |>
  arrange(tier) |> dt()
```

```{r spot-check-results}
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "Team spot-check results (data/manual/spotcheck.csv)"
sc_path <- file.path(DIR_MANUAL, "spotcheck.csv")
sc <- if (file.exists(sc_path)) readr::read_csv(sc_path, col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c"), show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL
tier_rows <- if (is.null(sc)) NULL else sc |>
  filter(str_detect(coalesce(section, ""), "^In "), coalesce(tool_tier, "") %in% c("1", "2", "3"),
         str_to_lower(str_squish(coalesce(verdict, ""))) %in% c("right", "wrong", "unsure"))
if (!is.null(tier_rows) && nrow(tier_rows) > 0) {
  tier_rows <- mutate(tier_rows, verdict = str_to_lower(str_squish(verdict)))
  cat(sprintf("**Tiers 1-3 spot-check:** the team checked %d opportunities by reading the announcements: %d right, %d wrong, %d unsure.\n",
              nrow(tier_rows), sum(tier_rows$verdict == "right"), sum(tier_rows$verdict == "wrong"), sum(tier_rows$verdict == "unsure")))
} else {
  cat("**Tiers 1-3 were not hand spot-checked.** We ran out of time before the team could read each announcement in the table above. The evidence for these tiers is the blind comparison with 60 hand labels in section 12: the facts that decide Tier 3 (match, construction, designation) agree over 90% of the time, while the capability judgments that separate Tier 1 from Tier 2 are weaker, so a writer should confirm a Tier 1 result before committing staff.\n")
}
```

## What the research rule may have killed

The research and NIH screen removes most of the haystack. The risk is that it removes something a
state agency could legitimately pursue. Among candidates the model labeled, these were flagged as
research mechanisms by the keyword rule but judged administrable by a state agency:

```{r research-killed}
#| code-summary: "Research-screened but judged administrable"
if (labels_ok) {
  grants |> filter(is_research_mechanism) |>
    inner_join(filter(labels, labeled, llm_administrable), by = "opportunity_number") |>
    transmute(opportunity = opportunity_title, agency = agency_code,
              `DHHS alignment` = llm_align_dhhs, evidence = llm_administrable_evidence) |> dt()
} else HTML('<div class="pending">Fills in when labeling finishes.</div>')
```

The tool keeps research awards visible (Tier 4, or the screened list when research is hidden) and
marks those in the top `r pct_fmt(1 - ALIGNMENT_RESCUE_PCT)` of plan alignment "check this".

**The team's review of the flagged research items.**

```{r research-review}
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "What reviewers said about research items flagged 'check this'"
if (!is.null(sc)) {
  rr <- sc |> filter(!str_detect(coalesce(section, ""), "^In "))
  said <- str_to_lower(paste(rr$verdict, rr$correct_tier))
  n_tier <- sum(str_detect(said, "research tier|new tier"))
  n_notrel <- sum(str_detect(said, "not relevant"))
  n_eval <- sum(str_detect(str_to_lower(paste(rr$verdict, rr$correct_tier, rr$notes)), "research_and_rigorous_evaluation"))
  cat(sprintf("Reviewers read %d research opportunities that the plan-alignment score flagged as worth a second look. For %d they recommended a separate research tier rather than treating them like program grants; %d %s judged not relevant; and %d were noted as requiring research and rigorous evaluation capacity, which DHHS reaches only through university partners. That is the design the tool uses: research awards form Tier 4, partner-led research, below the three authority tiers. None were judged to be programs DHHS could lead itself.\n",
              nrow(rr), n_tier, n_notrel, if (n_notrel == 1) "was" else "were", n_eval))
}
```

## Where the method misleads

Text-similarity alignment rewards shared vocabulary, not shared purpose. Scored against every row
of the DHHS plan, including rows about how the department runs itself, generic grant language
matches the plan's language about stewardship and staffing:

```{r misleads}
#| code-summary: "Alignment with and without internal-operations plan rows"
full <- compute_alignment(grants, load_priorities()) |> filter(agency == "DHHS")
prog <- alignment |> filter(agency == "DHHS")
cand <- grants |> filter(state_eligible, !is_nih, status_group == "Posted") |> pull(opportunity_number)
full |> select(opportunity_number, pct_all_rows = emb_pct, best_all_rows = emb_best_id) |>
  inner_join(select(prog, opportunity_number, pct_program_rows = emb_pct, best_program_rows = emb_best_id), by = "opportunity_number") |>
  filter(opportunity_number %in% cand) |>
  left_join(titles, by = "opportunity_number") |>
  mutate(shift = pct_all_rows - pct_program_rows) |>
  arrange(desc(shift)) |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(opportunity = opportunity_title, agency = agency_code,
            `percentile, all plan rows` = pct_fmt(pct_all_rows), `best row` = best_all_rows,
            `percentile, program rows only` = pct_fmt(pct_program_rows), `best row ` = best_program_rows) |>
  dt(dom = "t", pageLength = 12)
```

```{r similarity-vs-judgment}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| code-summary: "Text similarity against the model's alignment judgment"
if (labels_ok) {
  prog |> inner_join(filter(labels, labeled) |> select(opportunity_number, llm_align_dhhs), by = "opportunity_number") |>
    mutate(level = factor(str_to_sentence(llm_align_dhhs), levels = c("None", "Partial", "Strong"))) |>
    ggplot(aes(emb_pct, level)) +
    geom_boxplot(width = .5, outlier.shape = NA, fill = pal$blue_light, color = pal$blue) +
    geom_point(position = position_jitter(height = .12, width = 0, seed = SEED), alpha = .35, size = 1.4, color = pal$blue) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
    labs(title = "High similarity does not mean the model found a real link",
         subtitle = str_wrap("Embedding-similarity percentile against DHHS program rows, by the model's alignment rating", 80),
         x = "Similarity percentile", y = "Model's alignment") +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}
```

::: {.takeaway}
Opportunities the model rated *none* reach the top similarity percentiles too. Similarity is a
hint, never the decision.
:::

The table lists the opportunities whose ranking changed most when those rows were removed, with
the plan row each one matched. Rows marked internal operations describe how the department
runs itself (staffing, pay, contracting, buildings); grant boilerplate about staff, budgets and
partners resembles them closely, so opportunities with no health or human services content rose
toward the top. We
removed those rows from alignment scoring (`alignable = FALSE` in the plan tables) and made the
model's judgment, which must cite a plan row and explain the link, the deciding signal for which
agency sees an opportunity. Similarity scores remain only as a secondary hint.

# 16. Limitations

- **Match percentages are almost never published in structured form.** Only
  `r fact_val("Rows stating a match percentage anywhere in text")` of `r n_fmt(nrow(grants))`
  rows state one anywhere in the export, against `r fact_val("is_cost_sharing TRUE")` flagged as
  requiring cost share. The labeler reads full announcements where they exist
  (`r n_fmt(nofo_n)` of `r n_fmt(cand_n)` candidates); forecasts usually have none.
- **The capability profiles describe real agencies from public sources**, not interviews with
  agency staff. Every row is sourced and editable, but a division head would know better.
- **The appropriation line (`r usd_fmt(APPROPRIATION_THRESHOLD_USD)`) is an assumption.** No
  published NC rule sets it; the tool lets the user change it.
- **The local model is reliable on stated facts and weaker on judgment.** Against 60 blind hand
  labels it agrees on whether match is required `r pct_fmt(validation$summary$accuracy[validation$summary$field == "match required"])`
  of the time, but on whether a state agency could lead the program only
  `r pct_fmt(validation$summary$accuracy[validation$summary$field == "administrable"])`, on DHHS
  alignment `r pct_fmt(validation$summary$accuracy[validation$summary$field == "DHHS alignment"])`, and it
  finds only `r pct_fmt(validation$capabilities$recall)` of the capabilities the team listed. Missed
  capabilities mean missed partner needs, so some Tier 1 results probably belong in Tier 2. It also
  once wrote its own rule ("work happens outside the United States") into a field meant for a quote.
  It never assigns a tier, and every label it contributes is shown with its evidence (section 12).
- **Tiers 1-3 were not hand spot-checked.** The team reviewed the research awards but ran out of time
  to read each Tier 1-3 announcement; the blind hand-label comparison is the evidence for those tiers.
- **The eight domains have no veterans category.** Three hand labels used one; the model cannot
  choose it, and they count as disagreements.
- **Geography is domain-level.** County need describes where a program domain's need
  concentrates, not where a statewide grant would be spent. County overdose data are NCHS
  model-based estimates for `r min(OVERDOSE_YEARS)`-`r max(OVERDOSE_YEARS)`, the most recent years
  published; CDC WONDER's county-level counts need its web form and data-use agreement.
- **The snapshot ages.** `r n_fmt(closed_since)` posted opportunities had closed or been archived
  six weeks after the pull.
- **The DHHS plan is the one the competition provided (2023-2025, hosted by OSBM).** DHHS has
  since published 2024-2026 and 2026-2030 plans on its own site. The plan is an input table
  (`data/manual/dhhs_priorities.csv`), so updating it is a file swap followed by one re-labeling pass.
- **Community reach depends on the labeler's population choice.** The tool can show where the people
  an opportunity serves live, but 170 of the 210 labeled opportunities were marked "all residents" or
  "system-level", and some of those choices are too broad (the Preschool Development Grant is marked
  "all residents" rather than young children). District counts use the districts drawn for the 118th
  Congress; North Carolina redrew them for the 2024 election.
- **People-served estimates are upper bounds.** They count the population an opportunity serves in
  NC, not people an award would reach.

# 17. What we would build with more time

- Pull full announcements for every opportunity weekly and diff them, so match percentages and
  deadlines update themselves.
- Replace keyword and similarity alignment with the DMVA plan's own **Priority Questions**: an
  opportunity that helps answer a question the agency itself posed is a stronger match than one
  that shares vocabulary.
- Interview division staff to verify each capability's control level.
- Add past award history (USAspending) by assistance listing to estimate competitiveness.
- Let a supervisor pre-approve a match budget so Tier 2 items can move to Tier 1 in bulk.
- Add veterans as a cross-cutting flag rather than a ninth domain, so DMVA-relevant programs in any
  domain surface together.
- Improve capability extraction, the model's weakest measured field, by reading the full
  announcement's program requirements section rather than an excerpt.

# 19. Appendix: DMVA supplement

DMVA is a contrast case, not a parallel analysis. Its entire universe in this file is
`r sum(grants$is_va)` VA-issued opportunities, `r sum(grants$is_va & grants$status_group == "Forecasted")`
of them forecasts.

```{r dmva}
#| code-summary: "DMVA's opportunities, tiered as DMVA"
dmva_settings <- modifyList(payload$config$opening, list(agency = "DMVA", include_forecasts = TRUE))
run_tiering_js(opps, payload$capabilities$profiles, dmva_settings) |>
  inner_join(filter(grants, is_va) |> select(opportunity_number, opportunity_title, status_group,
                                             award_ceiling_clean, is_cost_sharing, applicant_types), by = "opportunity_number") |>
  transmute(opportunity = opportunity_title, status = status_group, ceiling = usd_fmt(award_ceiling_clean),
            `cost share` = is_cost_sharing, eligible = applicant_types, placement, tier, reason = coalesce(tier_reason, placement_why)) |>
  dt(dom = "t")
```

```{r dmva-goal}
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "The DMVA plan objective it maps to"
g <- load_priorities() |> filter(priority_id == "G2.O1", agency == "DMVA")
cat("> **DMVA Goal 2, Objective 1 (p. ", g$page, "):** ", g$text, "\n", sep = "")
```

The one posted DMVA opportunity, the State Veterans Home Construction Grant Program, matches
DMVA's own current goal of modernizing the veterans homes, and lands in Tier 3 because a capital
construction project with cost share needs an appropriation. The agency's best match is the thing
it cannot act on alone. The DMVA plan also lists explicit *Priority Questions*; aligning
opportunities to those questions is the natural next feature (section 17).
